paragraphs.heading: What a peptide bond is
paragraphs.text: A peptide bond is the link that joins one amino acid to the next along a peptide or protein chain. Chemists class it as an amide bond, a kind of covalent bond. It runs from carbon number one of one alpha-amino acid to nitrogen number two of the next. These bonds hold the amino acids of peptides and proteins in a chain, at times alongside a few isopeptide bonds, which are a different kind of amide link.

paragraphs.heading: How two amino acids join
paragraphs.text: Joining two amino acids this way is a condensation reaction. The carboxylic acid end of one comes close to the amino end of the other. One amino acid gives up a hydrogen and an oxygen from its COOH group, and the other gives up a hydrogen from its NH₂ group. Those pieces leave together as one molecule of H₂O, and the two amino acids are left joined by a −CO−NH− link. The pair is called a dipeptide, and because water is released the process counts as dehydration synthesis.

paragraphs.heading: Who builds them
paragraphs.text: Making a peptide bond takes energy, and in living things that energy comes from ATP. Cells build proteins on ribosomes, and build some other peptides with dedicated enzymes, using reactions whose details differ from plain dehydration synthesis. The small peptide glutathione, for example, is put together from free amino acids in two steps by two enzymes. One enzyme forms an isopeptide bond and the other forms a true peptide bond.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking it
paragraphs.text: Adding water can split a peptide bond, a reaction called hydrolysis. It releases 8–16 kJ/mol of Gibbs energy, yet on its own it is extremely slow. At 25 °C, each bond has a half-life of 350 to 600 years. In living things, enzymes called peptidases or proteases normally speed the job up.

paragraphs.heading: A flat, stiff link
paragraphs.text: The nitrogen's lone pair of electrons spreads out across the bond, giving it partly the character of a double bond. This keeps the amide group flat, and it can sit in one of two arrangements, cis or trans. The trans form wins by a wide margin, at roughly 1000 to 1 in most peptide bonds. For X-Pro peptide groups, which involve the amino acid proline, the split is closer, at roughly 30 to 1.

paragraphs.heading: Flipping slows folding
paragraphs.text: Switching a peptide bond between cis and trans is slow, taking about 20 seconds at room temperature. Protein folding is usually far quicker, typically 10–100 ms, compared with 10–100 s for the switch. If a bond is stuck in the wrong form, it can slow folding badly or stop it until the right form is reached. Living things have enzymes called peptidyl prolyl isomerases that speed up this switch at X-Pro bonds.

paragraphs.heading: Tough but not untouchable
paragraphs.text: Because of its resonance stabilization, the peptide bond reacts little under the conditions inside the body, even less than related compounds such as esters. It can still react when an electronegative atom attacks its carbonyl carbon and forms a tetrahedral intermediate, the route taken when proteins are cut apart. The bond also absorbs light at wavelengths of 190–230 nm, which leaves it especially open to damage from UV radiation.
